definition: A set of software-development values and principles that favor collaboration, working outcomes, customer partnership, and adaptation over rigid process compliance.
practicalMeaning: In practice, agile means building feedback into planning and delivery so evidence can change both the product and the way the team works.
example: A team releases a small usable improvement, reviews user behavior, and changes its next priority from what it learned.

definition: A lightweight framework for complex product development with defined accountabilities, events, artifacts, commitments, and short inspect-and-adapt cycles.
practicalMeaning: Scrum gives a stable team a regular rhythm for pursuing a Product Goal while changing the detailed plan as new evidence appears.
example: A Scrum Team chooses a Sprint Goal, creates a usable Increment, reviews it with stakeholders, then improves its process.

definition: A fixed-length Scrum event of one month or less during which the Scrum Team works toward a Sprint Goal and creates a usable Increment.
practicalMeaning: The Sprint protects a short planning and learning horizon; it is not a promise that every selected backlog item will remain unchanged.
example: During a two-week Sprint, developers adapt tasks while preserving the goal of enabling members to submit an application.

definition: An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve a product and the single source of work undertaken by a Scrum Team.
practicalMeaning: A healthy Product Backlog communicates direction and choices; it is refined as evidence changes rather than becoming a permanent request warehouse.
example: The Product Owner reorders identity verification above profile customization because it blocks the next measurable outcome.

definition: A long-term objective for a Scrum Team that describes a future state of the product and gives the Product Backlog a coherent direction.
practicalMeaning: The Product Goal helps the team reject unrelated work and evaluate whether increments are moving toward a meaningful product outcome.
example: The team sets a Product Goal to let association staff manage membership applications without developer support.

definition: The single objective for a Scrum Sprint that explains why the work is valuable and gives Developers flexibility in how they achieve it.
practicalMeaning: When individual tasks change, the Sprint Goal remains the decision anchor for collaboration, scope trade-offs, and daily adaptation.
example: The Sprint Goal is “members can complete and confirm an application,” even if one optional profile field is postponed.

definition: A formal description of the quality state an Increment must meet before it is considered complete and usable within Scrum.
practicalMeaning: It creates shared transparency about quality, preventing teams from calling partially integrated or untested work complete.
example: A feature is done only after review, automated tests, accessibility checks, documentation, and deployment to the agreed environment.

definition: A concrete usable step toward a product goal that adds to all previous work and meets the applicable quality definition.
practicalMeaning: An Increment is integrated product behavior, not a collection of separate design, coding, and testing tasks waiting for later assembly.
example: A completed membership confirmation flow is usable end to end and can be released even if other profile features wait.

definition: A structured reflection in which a team inspects how work happened and agrees on changes intended to improve quality and effectiveness.
practicalMeaning: A retrospective should produce honest learning and a small completed improvement, not become a recurring meeting for complaints without ownership.
example: The team limits concurrent review work after discovering that large pull-request queues caused repeated release delays.

definition: A strategy for optimizing the flow of value through a process by defining workflow, controlling work in progress, actively managing items, and improving.
practicalMeaning: Kanban makes queues, aging, blockage, and policies visible so a service can become faster and more predictable without prescribing new job titles.
example: A support team limits investigations in progress and swarms on aging incidents before pulling new requests.

definition: Work that has started but has not yet reached the defined finished state of a workflow or service.
practicalMeaning: Limiting work in progress reduces multitasking and queues, creates pressure to finish, and exposes where the system cannot absorb more work.
example: The team stops starting a sixth feature because its WIP limit is five and instead helps finish a blocked review.

definition: The elapsed time from when a work item starts in a defined workflow until it reaches the workflow’s finished state.
practicalMeaning: Teams use cycle-time distributions to understand delivery speed and predictability rather than relying only on optimistic estimates.
example: Most small fixes finish in two to five days, but the team investigates items aging beyond eight days.

definition: The count of work items completed by a workflow or service during a defined period of time.
practicalMeaning: Throughput helps teams understand actual delivery capacity, especially when interpreted with item size, quality, demand, and cycle time.
example: The service completes between 18 and 24 comparable support requests per week over the last three months.

definition: A forecast describing how long a work item should take to flow from start to finish with an explicit probability or confidence level.
practicalMeaning: An SLE guides conversations about aging work and customer expectations; it is a forecast based on evidence rather than a guaranteed deadline.
example: The team expects 85 percent of standard requests to finish within seven days once work begins.

definition: A predictive delivery model that moves work through substantially sequential phases such as requirements, design, implementation, verification, and release.
practicalMeaning: Waterfall can support formal traceability and expensive sequential dependencies, but late feedback becomes dangerous when needs or feasibility are uncertain.
example: A regulated system completes approved requirements and design baselines before controlled implementation and verification phases begin.

definition: Documented needs, capabilities, constraints, qualities, or conditions that a product, service, or system is expected to satisfy.
practicalMeaning: Requirements are useful when they make purpose and acceptance testable; they become harmful when assumptions are presented as permanent facts.
example: A requirement states that only authorized editors may publish an article and that every publication action must be auditable.

definition: A significant zero-duration checkpoint used to represent an important event, approval, dependency, or delivery state in a plan.
practicalMeaning: Milestones help coordinate expectations but should describe meaningful evidence rather than arbitrary calendar decoration.
example: “Client acceptance completed” is a milestone supported by signed evidence, while “development 80% complete” is not.

definition: A governed process for recording, assessing, approving, and communicating changes to an agreed scope, baseline, system, or operational state.
practicalMeaning: Good change control makes impact and accountability visible without pretending that change itself is a failure.
example: A requested integration change is assessed for cost, security, schedule, and testing impact before the project baseline is updated.

definition: Specific conditions used to determine whether a work item or product behavior satisfies the intended need and can be accepted.
practicalMeaning: Acceptance criteria create a shared testable understanding, but they do not replace discovery, design judgment, or broader quality standards.
example: The application displays a confirmation reference, sends an email, and prevents a duplicate submission after success.

definition: An informal hybrid that combines selected Scrum goals or cadences with Kanban workflow visualization, pull, work-in-progress control, and flow measures.
practicalMeaning: Teams should document which rules they retain; otherwise Scrumban can become an unclear mix of ceremonies and ad hoc priorities.
example: A team keeps a two-week product goal but replenishes tasks continuously within explicit WIP limits.

definition: An ordered or categorized collection of potential work, requests, defects, opportunities, or obligations that has not yet been completed.
practicalMeaning: A backlog is a decision aid, not a promise to deliver every item; stale and low-value entries should be removed or reconsidered.
example: The team archives requests that no longer support its strategy instead of carrying them indefinitely as hidden commitments.

definition: A communication view of intended product direction, outcomes, themes, or investments across time rather than a guaranteed feature schedule.
practicalMeaning: A useful roadmap explains strategic choices and uncertainty while connecting near-term work to measurable outcomes.
example: The quarterly roadmap groups work under member growth, editorial efficiency, and platform reliability instead of listing every ticket.

definition: A person or group that affects, is affected by, or has a legitimate interest in a product, service, project, or decision.
practicalMeaning: Stakeholder management means understanding influence, impact, needs, evidence, and decision rights—not merely sending everyone status updates.
example: Editors, members, funders, support staff, and developers are different stakeholders in a new publishing workflow.

definition: A brief product-backlog expression of a need from a user perspective, usually intended to support conversation rather than replace detailed understanding.
practicalMeaning: A story is valuable when it connects context, desired outcome, examples, and collaboration; filling a template alone does not create insight.
example: An editor needs to preview an article before publication so formatting problems are found without exposing drafts publicly.

definition: The smallest product experiment or release capable of testing a meaningful value assumption with real users and credible evidence.
practicalMeaning: An MVP is not the lowest-quality version of a large roadmap; it intentionally narrows scope while preserving the core learning question.
example: Instead of building a full marketplace, a team tests whether users request curated matches through a simple assisted workflow.

definition: A management approach focused on customer value, end-to-end value streams, flow, pull, quality, respect for people, and continuous improvement.
practicalMeaning: Lean asks teams to improve the whole system rather than maximize local utilization or treat cost cutting as the only goal.
example: A team maps request-to-release delay and removes an approval queue that adds no risk reduction or customer value.

definition: The complete sequence of activities and information required to respond to demand and deliver a product or service outcome to a customer.
practicalMeaning: Mapping a value stream exposes delay, handoffs, rework, and missing feedback that individual team metrics often hide.
example: The map covers idea intake, discovery, design, coding, review, deployment, support, and product feedback.

definition: The smooth movement of work or value through a defined system with minimal waiting, blockage, rework, batching, and unnecessary handoff.
practicalMeaning: Improving flow usually means finishing more consistently with less concurrent work, not making every individual appear fully utilized.
example: Reviewers swarm on open changes so completed features reach users instead of accumulating in a queue.

definition: A work system in which new activity begins in response to real demand and available downstream capacity rather than forecast-driven overproduction.
practicalMeaning: Pull protects flow by preventing teams from starting work that the next step cannot absorb or finish.
example: A developer selects a new ready item only after a review slot becomes available under the workflow limit.

definition: An ongoing disciplined practice of studying work, testing changes, learning from outcomes, and standardizing useful improvements over time.
practicalMeaning: The important unit is a completed improvement with evidence, not a growing list of retrospective ideas that nobody owns.
example: The team changes its release checklist, measures rollback failures for a month, and keeps or adjusts the change from results.

definition: An agile software-development method centered on rapid feedback and reinforcing engineering practices such as testing, pairing, refactoring, and continuous integration.
practicalMeaning: XP makes adaptation technically sustainable by keeping code integrated, tested, understandable, and collectively owned.
example: Two developers pair on a small story, write tests first, integrate it the same day, and refactor before selecting the next story.

definition: A development practice that cycles through writing a failing automated test, making it pass with minimal code, and improving the design through refactoring.
practicalMeaning: TDD uses tests to guide small design decisions and produce fast regression feedback; it is not a substitute for every other testing method.
example: A developer first expresses the rejected duplicate application as a failing unit test, then implements and refactors the rule.

definition: A collaborative development practice in which two people work together at one workstation or shared environment on the same software task.
practicalMeaning: Pairing combines real-time design, review, knowledge sharing, and problem solving, with participants switching active and observing roles intentionally.
example: One engineer writes a migration while the other checks data assumptions and rollback safety, then they swap roles.

definition: Changing the internal structure of existing software without intentionally changing its externally observable behavior.
practicalMeaning: Refactoring keeps future change safer and clearer when performed in small steps with reliable tests and an explicit design purpose.
example: After tests pass, repeated validation logic is moved into one named function without altering application results.

definition: A repository workflow object proposing that one set of version-controlled changes be reviewed and merged into another branch.
practicalMeaning: A pull request is a collaboration and quality checkpoint containing context, evidence, discussion, and traceability—not just permission to merge code.
example: The author explains the membership-state change, links the issue, includes test evidence, and requests review from the data owner.

definition: A systematic examination of source-code changes by people or automated controls to find defects, improve design, and share knowledge.
practicalMeaning: Effective review prioritizes correctness, risk, maintainability, security, and learning rather than formatting debates already handled by tools.
example: A reviewer notices that an authorization check exists in the interface but not in the API and requests a server-side fix.

definition: A defined contract through which software components or external systems request capabilities, exchange data, or receive events.
practicalMeaning: A stable API makes responsibilities, inputs, outputs, errors, permissions, and change expectations explicit for its consumers.
example: The membership API accepts validated application data and returns a reference identifier or a documented error response.

definition: A server-side software component that exposes business capabilities, manages data or integrations, and runs independently of a user interface.
practicalMeaning: A service should own a coherent responsibility and operational contract rather than becoming an arbitrary collection of endpoints.
example: The notification service receives approved events, renders messages, sends email, and records delivery status.

definition: The process of establishing or verifying the identity of a user, service, or device before granting identity-dependent access.
practicalMeaning: Authentication answers who or what is making a request; authorization separately decides what that identity may do.
example: An editor signs in with a verified account before the system evaluates whether they may publish content.

definition: The process of deciding whether an authenticated identity has permission to perform a specific action on a resource or within a context.
practicalMeaning: Authorization must be enforced at trusted system boundaries, not only by hiding interface controls from users.
example: The API permits editors to save drafts but only administrators to change another user’s role.

definition: The future cost and reduced flexibility created by technical choices, shortcuts, missing maintenance, or system conditions that make change harder.
practicalMeaning: Debt should be described through concrete impact, risk, and options rather than used as a vague label for code someone dislikes.
example: Duplicated authorization rules cause inconsistent fixes, so the team consolidates them before adding another role.

definition: A maintained collection of reusable design decisions, components, patterns, standards, documentation, and contribution practices for product teams.
practicalMeaning: A design system aligns design and code while reducing repeated decisions; a component library alone is only one part of the system.
example: The system defines accessible button behavior, visual tokens, coded components, usage guidance, and review ownership.

definition: A representation of a possible product or service used to explore, communicate, or test assumptions before committing to full implementation.
practicalMeaning: Prototype fidelity should match the question: a sketch can test flow, while interactive behavior may require a coded or high-fidelity model.
example: The team tests whether editors understand the publishing sequence using a clickable prototype before building APIs.

definition: Structured work that reduces uncertainty about users, problems, value, feasibility, constraints, and potential solution directions before or during delivery.
practicalMeaning: Discovery does not guarantee certainty; it produces enough credible evidence to make a better next investment or test.
example: Researchers observe editorial work while engineers test integration feasibility and product compares outcome options.

definition: A focused evidence-based explanation of who experiences a problem, in what context, why it matters, and what constraints shape a useful outcome.
practicalMeaning: A strong definition guides solution exploration without disguising a preferred feature as the problem itself.
example: Instead of “we need notifications,” the brief states that applicants cannot tell whether submissions were received or what happens next.

definition: A concise shared statement of a design challenge, audience, intended outcome, evidence, constraints, scope, and decision conditions.
practicalMeaning: The brief translates discovery into a usable direction while remaining open enough for multiple solution approaches.
example: The team agrees to reduce failed mobile applications without changing the required legal fields or exposing private data.

definition: A design-process model with alternating divergence and convergence across Discover, Define, Develop, and Deliver phases.
practicalMeaning: It reminds teams to explore evidence and multiple possibilities before converging, while allowing iteration rather than enforcing a rigid sequence.
example: The team researches many causes, defines one priority problem, prototypes several approaches, then implements and measures one.

definition: The quality of products, services, and environments being usable by people with diverse abilities, technologies, contexts, and access needs.
practicalMeaning: Accessibility is a design and engineering requirement throughout discovery, content, interaction, implementation, testing, and maintenance.
example: A form supports keyboard use, visible focus, understandable errors, screen-reader labels, zoom, and sufficient contrast.

definition: A socio-technical approach that joins software development and operation through shared responsibility, automation, fast feedback, and continuous learning.
practicalMeaning: DevOps is an organizational capability, not merely a team name, cloud role, or collection of pipeline tools.
example: A product team owns deployment, telemetry, incident learning, and improvements with support from a platform team.

definition: A practice in which developers integrate small changes into a shared codebase frequently and receive fast automated build and test feedback.
practicalMeaning: CI reduces integration risk by making incompatibility visible early and keeping the main code line in a healthy state.
example: Each pull request runs formatting, type, unit, integration, and security checks before a small merge.

definition: The capability to keep software in a releasable state through automated, repeatable build, verification, configuration, and deployment practices.
practicalMeaning: Continuous delivery means a safe release can be made on demand; it does not require exposing every successful build to all users immediately.
example: A verified immutable artifact can be promoted to production through an automated pipeline with rollback and audit evidence.

definition: A common shorthand for continuous integration and continuous delivery or deployment practices that automate feedback and software release flow.
practicalMeaning: The label only has value when pipelines make change safer, faster, traceable, and repeatable rather than adding fragile automation.
example: A commit creates a tested artifact, deploys it to preview, and allows controlled production promotion after required checks.

definition: The technical act of installing, configuring, or activating a software version and its dependencies in a target environment.
practicalMeaning: Deployment and release can be separated: code may be safely deployed while a feature remains hidden or gradually enabled.
example: Version 2.4 is deployed to production, but the new editor remains behind a feature flag for internal users.

definition: The product or business decision to make a capability available to intended users, customers, or operational consumers.
practicalMeaning: Separating release from deployment enables safer experiments, staged exposure, and independent operational control.
example: The team releases the already-deployed workflow to ten percent of members and watches support and completion data.

definition: A configurable control that changes whether a software capability is enabled for selected users, environments, or conditions without a new deployment.
practicalMeaning: Flags support gradual release and experiments, but unmanaged flags create complexity and must have ownership and removal plans.
example: The new checkout is enabled for staff accounts first, then gradually expanded while error rates are monitored.

definition: A controlled action that restores a previous known software, configuration, data, or infrastructure state after an unsafe change.
practicalMeaning: Rollback readiness reduces recovery time, but data migrations and external effects may require forward fixes or explicit recovery plans.
example: After elevated errors, the deployment pipeline restores the previous application image while the incident team investigates.

definition: The ability to understand a system’s internal state and behavior from its outputs, context, and intentionally designed telemetry.
practicalMeaning: Observability helps teams ask new questions during unexpected conditions instead of relying only on predetermined alert checks.
example: Engineers correlate a user request across logs, metrics, and traces to find latency in an external service.

definition: Automatically collected signals about software, infrastructure, user interaction, or operational processes used for observation and analysis.
practicalMeaning: Telemetry should be purposeful, privacy-aware, and connected to decisions rather than collected without ownership or retention limits.
example: The service records request latency, error type, deployment version, and anonymous completion events for a critical flow.

definition: An unplanned event that degrades or threatens a service, user outcome, security property, or agreed operational condition.
practicalMeaning: Incident management coordinates stabilization, communication, investigation, and learning; it should not focus on finding one person to blame.
example: A deployment prevents members from submitting forms, triggering response, rollback, stakeholder updates, and a follow-up review.

definition: A target level of service reliability or performance measured by a defined service-level indicator over a specified period.
practicalMeaning: SLOs turn vague reliability expectations into explicit trade-offs between product change, risk, and operational investment.
example: The team targets 99.9 percent successful membership submissions measured over a rolling 28-day window.

definition: The permitted amount of unreliability implied by a service-level objective during its measurement window.
practicalMeaning: Teams use the remaining budget to balance release speed and reliability work instead of demanding impossible perfect availability.
example: After consuming most of the monthly budget, the team pauses risky launches and prioritizes failure prevention.

definition: An uncertain event or condition that could affect an objective, often considered through likelihood, impact, exposure, and response options.
practicalMeaning: Useful risk work identifies specific scenarios, owners, triggers, mitigations, and residual exposure rather than maintaining generic red lists.
example: The team reduces data-loss risk through backups, restore tests, access controls, and a documented recovery owner.

definition: The possibility that a threat exploits a vulnerability and causes harm to confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, privacy, or organizational outcomes.
practicalMeaning: Security risk should be evaluated in context so controls are proportionate and remediation priorities reflect credible harm.
example: Public file uploads could execute active content, so the service validates type, stores files separately, and serves safe responses.

definition: A product-development method based on shaping bounded work, setting an appetite, selecting bets, fixed build cycles, variable scope, and team autonomy.
practicalMeaning: Shape Up shifts detailed task discovery to the builder team while requiring senior shaping to remove major risks before commitment.
example: Leaders select a six-week bet with clear boundaries, and the team cuts optional scope rather than extending the cycle.

definition: The amount of time and attention an organization is willing to invest in a problem before designing or committing to a solution.
practicalMeaning: An appetite is a strategic constraint that shapes the solution; it is not an estimate of a fully specified scope.
example: The team gives notification improvements a two-week appetite and designs a narrow solution that fits that investment.

definition: A shaped proposal describing a problem, appetite, solution direction, boundaries, risks, and no-gos for a potential product bet.
practicalMeaning: The pitch supplies enough context for a team to exercise judgment without turning the work into a prewritten task list.
example: The pitch explains the publishing delay, sketches the key interaction, identifies permission risk, and excludes analytics redesign.

definition: A repeated bounded period used by a method or organization to plan, build, review, learn, or allocate capacity.
practicalMeaning: The meaning depends on the method; teams should state whether a cycle is a fixed delivery bet, a Sprint, or simply a reporting period.
example: A Shape Up team receives one six-week build cycle followed by cooldown, while another team uses two-week Sprints.

definition: A Shape Up progress visualization that distinguishes work still being figured out from work that has a known execution path.
practicalMeaning: Moving uphill represents uncertainty reduction; moving downhill represents completing understood work, making unknowns more visible than percent complete.
example: A team keeps permissions uphill while the editor interface moves downhill because its remaining tasks are understood.

definition: A team that provides internal capabilities and services intended to reduce cognitive load and accelerate safe delivery for product-oriented teams.
practicalMeaning: A platform should behave like an internal product with clear users, supported paths, documentation, feedback, and measured usefulness.
example: The platform team offers a supported deployment pipeline, secrets management, logs, and templates that product teams can self-serve.

definition: A team containing the complementary skills and authority needed to pursue an outcome without routine handoffs to separate functional departments.
practicalMeaning: Cross-functional does not mean every member has every skill; it means the team can collaborate across necessary disciplines and owns an integrated result.
example: A product team includes product, design, frontend, backend, and quality capabilities needed to improve membership onboarding.

definition: An explicit description of a team’s purpose, responsibilities, supported services, communication channels, boundaries, and ways other teams interact with it.
practicalMeaning: A Team API reduces hidden dependency and helps collaborators choose self-service, facilitation, or close collaboration intentionally.
example: The platform team documents supported deployment paths, response expectations, escalation channels, and unsupported custom infrastructure.

definition: The boundaries of work, outcomes, features, systems, responsibilities, or conditions included and excluded from an initiative or decision.
practicalMeaning: Scope should be explicit and changeable through informed trade-offs; ambiguity creates hidden commitments and conflicting expectations.
example: The release includes application submission and confirmation but excludes payment and member-directory profiles.

definition: The collection and analysis of behavioral and outcome data to understand how people use a product and whether changes create intended value.
practicalMeaning: Product analytics should begin with decisions and ethical measurement, then combine quantitative patterns with qualitative context.
example: The team compares completion, abandonment, error, and support-contact rates before and after redesigning an application flow.

definition: Systematic study of people, contexts, behavior, needs, and experiences to inform product or service decisions.
practicalMeaning: Research uses suitable methods and ethical practice to reduce uncertainty; it does not ask participants to become product strategists.
example: A researcher observes editors publishing real content and tests a prototype with representative users.
